title: The Jevons Paradox of AI Code
content:
The Jevons Paradox of AI Code
In 1865, a young English economist named William Stanley Jevons published a book that thoroughly detailed a counter-intuitive observation he made: when steam engines became more efficient, coal consumption did not fall, it skyrocketed. Efficiency lowered the price, unlocking massive new demand.
The Industrial Revolution was running on coal, and conventional wisdom held that as engineers designed more fuel-efficient steam engines, Britain’s finite coal reserves would be conserved. Jevons observed the exact opposite. When James Watt introduced a steam engine that consumed vastly less coal per unit of work, Britain’s total coal consumption did not decline. It exploded.
By making the steam engine dramatically cheaper to operate, Watt unlocked countless new industrial applications that were previously economically nonviable. Demand surged, outstripping the efficiency gains. This counter-intuitive dynamic became known to economic history as Jevons’ Paradox: an increase in efficiency in using a resource leads to an overall increase in the consumption of that resource.
And if this sounds applicable to the modern day of software industry, it is. A century and a half later, we are stumbling headlong into the exact same trap. The tech industry’s prevailing narrative promises that automated code generation—powered by large language models, will dramatically shrink codebases, streamline engineering headcounts, and eliminate the friction of building software. The logic seems airtight on paper: if typing syntax becomes ten times faster, building systems must become ten times cheaper.
This I believe spawns from the core misunderstanding of what software is. Code is not an asset as balance sheets like to classify. I hear often lines of code written or shipped are treated as proof of productivity. However, in factual reality every line of code deployed to production is an active operational liability.
A line of code is a surface area for security vulnerabilities. It is a vector for state corruption. It is an obstacle to future architectural refactoring. Most critically, it is an ongoing cognitive tax levied against every engineer who will ever have to read, maintain, or debug that system over the next five years.
When you introduce tools that make syntax generation essentially frictionless, you do not magically reduce the cost of running a software organization. You simply lower the marginal cost of manufacturing liabilities
So what now? Can we learn something from the industrial revolution? How did we survive increased efficiency and energy demands? I'll leave it up to you to research this chapter in human history, but it was not painless. But no significant change is painless...
But I digress. Message I'm trying to convey is that surviving software engineers of the next decade will not be the prompt whisperers who brag about generating thousands of lines before lunchtime. Instead it will be the ones who possess the rare discipline, economic clarity, and systems craftsmanship to practice subtraction.
AI is a staggering amplifier. However, when applied carelessly to bypass the arduous process of learning how systems actually fail, it does not democratize software engineering, it merely automates the production of technical bankruptcy.
As Jevons proved with coal, abundance does not eliminate scarcity, it simply reveals what is truly scarce. In software, that scarcity will always be human discernment, architectural restraint, and the courage to write less.

report.summary: AI code generation may echo Jevons' Paradox: cheaper code production could multiply code volume and long-term maintenance liabilities rather than shrink engineering costs.
report.background: In 1865, William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines lowered operating costs, unlocked new industrial uses and caused total coal consumption to rise rather than fall — a counter-intuitive effect now called Jevons' Paradox. The article argues AI-assisted coding follows the same pattern. The dominant industry narrative promises that LLM code generation will shrink codebases, reduce headcount and make software cheaper to build. But the author contends this misreads what code is: not an asset on a balance sheet but an operational liability. Every deployed line is a potential vulnerability, a corruption vector, a barrier to refactoring and a persistent cognitive tax on every engineer who must later read and debug it. Frictionless syntax generation, in this view, does not cut the cost of running engineering organizations — it just lowers the marginal cost of manufacturing liabilities.
key_points: Jevons' Paradox in one line: efficiency gains often increase total resource use, not reduce it. Watt's coal-saving engine made steam power so cheap that new factories, railways and mills adopted it, and Britain burned far more coal overall than before.

The article rejects the metric of lines written or shipped as a proxy for productivity. Code is treated as an asset on balance sheets, but once deployed it functions as a liability that somebody must maintain, secure and eventually refactor.

Cheap code generation attacks only the typing step, not the expensive parts of software: requirements, architecture, testing, debugging and long-term ownership. Faster syntax production therefore mainly accelerates the creation of future maintenance work.

The author argues the surviving engineers of the next decade will not be prolific prompt writers but practitioners of 'subtraction' — people with the discipline and systems judgment to remove code, constrain scope and say no to unnecessary complexity.

AI is described as an amplifier: used carelessly to skip the hard learning of how systems fail, it automates technical debt and does not truly democratize engineering. Abundance reveals what is actually scarce — human discernment and architectural restraint.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a warning that code-generation benchmarks measuring speed and volume miss downstream cost. Vendors that can show measurable maintainability, review quality or reduced incident load will differentiate from raw autocomplete. For developers, the premium shifts from writing code quickly toward reviewing, deleting and owning systems — skills AI amplifies rather than replaces, and the ones least likely to be automated. For regular users, the practical effect is indirect but real: more software will exist, but quality and security may lag if generation outpaces review, so expect more frequent bugs, patches and data incidents in AI-heavy products before engineering discipline catches up.
report.tools: To follow this thread, watch code-health and static-analysis tools that quantify liabilities rather than output: CodeScene (code health and hotspots), SonarQube and Semgrep (security and rule-based scanning), jscpd or PMD CPD (duplication detection), and Ruff or Sourcery for simplification. On the AI review side, CodeRabbit and Qodo add automated review guardrails around generated code. Pair these with Dependabot for dependency pruning and track lines-deleted alongside lines-added as your real productivity metric.
